newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin meets Chinese, Indian leaders.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin meets Chinese, Indian leaders.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin put aside domestic problems on Tuesday to give a warm welcome to high-level visitors from India and China which Moscow sees as potential partners in the post Cold War world.
Yeltsin told Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda that Moscow was committed to maintaining close relations with New Delhi which it considers to have a key role in Asia.
"We have been friends for many decades and we remain friends," Yeltsin told Deve Gowda. "India remains a stabilising force in its region."

Russian news agencies said on Monday that Yeltsin, who is completing a dramatic cabinet reshuffle aimed at boosting stalled economic reform, had postponed his traditional weekly meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to focus on talks with Deve Gowda and Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen.
On Tuesday, instead of meeting Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin met Deve Gowda and then Qian, who came to prepare a visit by Chinese President Ziang Zemin planned for late April.
Qian also met Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov. Both Asian visitors are also due to hold talks with Chernomyrdin, whose weekly meeting with Yeltsin was resheduled for Wednesday.

Deve Gowda and Qian are visiting Moscow days after Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton "agreed to disagree" over NATO's plans to invite former Soviet bloc states to join the Western defence alliance at their meeting in the Finnish capital Helsinki.

Russian officials say NATO's commitment to expansion, despite Moscow's objections, marks the end of the honeymoon period between Russia and the West which followed the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.
Russia is now looking for allies elsewhere. China and India, which also have strains in their relations with the West, are among the most highly prized partners.
Some Russian officials have indicated that NATO expansion had given a special flavour to Deve Gowda's and Qian's visits.

"Relations with India have strong roots and a broad base of common...interests in the world politics and economy," Itar-Tass news agency quoted deputy Defence Minister Andrei Kokoshin as saying on Monday.
"Moscow and New Delhi have similar positions as far as NATO eastward expansion is concerned," he said. "It is noteworthy that the Chinese leadership has a similar position."
Moscow has traditionally had close relations with India, especially strong in the 1960s and 1970s when New Delhi was involved in conflicts with China and U.S. ally Pakistan.

The weakness of post-Soviet Russia made special relations with it less attractive for India. But bilateral links have started improving lately as Russia has begun focusing more on relations with traditional partners to its south and east.
Russian officials have said that Deve Gowda's visit will have military and techinical cooperation high on agenda with Moscow planning to move ahead with some arms sales.

Detailed figures of Russian-Indian arms trade are not officially published. But military officials have said that last year's $1.8 billion contract to sell India 40 modern SU-30MK jet fighters was the biggest between them so far.

In contrast with India, Beijing and Moscow formed a strong alliance in the early 1950s which later degenerated into bitter rivalry for leadership of the world communist movement and led to border clashes in the late 1960s.
Relations have improved dramatically since a visit to Beijing by Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev in 1989.
Russia and China say they are keen to develop a strategic partnership in the 21st century, but both countries rule out the renewal of any military or political bloc.
During his visit to Russia in late April, Jiang is expected to sign a treaty with No details of the treaty have been revealed.
